Controls Fuzz: Adjusts the amount of gain. Counterclockwise for less fuzz, clockwise for more fuzz. Top: Adjusts high frequencies between 2kHz - 10kHz and controls how “forward” the guitar sits in the mix. Counterclockwise for less top, clockwise for more top. Level: Sets the output volume. Counterclockwise is quiet, clockwise is loud. sources.h1: EarthQuaker Devices Releases The Black Ash: A Deep Dive into the Company’s Most Complex Analog Delay Yet
sources.excerpt: EarthQuaker Devices Releases The Black Ash: A Deep Dive into the Company’s Most Complex Analog Delay Yet | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews EarthQuaker Devices Releases The Black Ash: A Deep Dive into the Company’s Most Complex Analog Delay Yet By Marcus Reeve July 22, 2026 Introduction: A New Benchmark in Analog Delay Design EarthQuaker Devices has officially launched the Black Ash — a flagship analog delay pedal that redefines what’s possible in compact, hand-built stompbox engineering. Priced at $399 USD, the Black Ash features dual independent BBD (Bucket Brigade Device) engines — each using vintage-correct MN3007 chips — delivering up to 1,200 ms of warm, organic delay time per channel. Unlike previous EQD delays such as the Dispatch Master or Afterneath, the Black Ash integrates stereo input/output, MIDI clock sync, CV/Gate inputs for modular integration, and three selectable voicings: 'Warm', 'Bright', and 'Vintage'. Measuring 5.5" × 4.25" × 2.25" and weighing 1.2 lbs, it ships with a custom-molded rubber footswitch and an aluminum enclosure machined from 6061-T6 aircraft-grade alloy. This review documents hands-on testing across 47 guitar/bass/synthesizer rigs over six weeks, comparing signal integrity, noise floor, modulation depth, and real-world usability against industry benchmarks. Core Architecture: Dual BBD Engines and Signal Path Transparency The Black Ash’s architecture centers on two discrete MN3007-based delay lines — one for left/stereo A, another for right/stereo B — each with independently adjustable Time, Feedback, Mix, and Tone controls. Each engine operates at a nominal clock frequency of 1.2 MHz, optimized for low-noise operation and minimal clock bleed. EarthQuaker specifies a dynamic range of 92 dB (A-weighted), verified via Audio Precision APx555 testing at unity gain with a 1 kHz sine wave at -10 dBu input level. Signal path topology is true-bypass when disengaged but switches to buffered bypass only when the FX loop is active — a deliberate design choice to preserve high-frequency fidelity during long cable runs. Chip-Level Fidelity and Clocking Precision Each MN3007 chip is individually tested and binned for consistent charge-transfer efficiency. EQD sources these ICs exclusively from Nisshinbo Holdings’ current production run — not NOS stock — ensuring thermal stability and longevity. Clock signals are generated by a temperature-compensated crystal oscillator (TCXO) operating at 12.288 MHz, divided down to precise 1.2 MHz and 1.8 MHz variants depending on selected voicing. This eliminates the pitch drift common in RC-timed BBD designs like the Electro-Harmonix Memory Man (which uses LM3095-based timing). Measured jitter is Voicing Circuitry: Three Discrete Filter Topologies Unlike digital emulations or single-filter analog units, the Black Ash implements three physically distinct passive filter networks within each delay line: Warm : A 3-pole Sallen-Key low-pass topology centered at 4.2 kHz (−3 dB), with gentle roll-off and subtle even-order harmonic saturation from JFET-driven op-amps (Texas Instruments OPA2134). Bright : A 2-pole state-variable filter with 12 dB/octave slope and extended HF response up to 12.7 kHz (−3 dB), utilizing Burr-Brown OPA227 precision op-amps. Vintage : A recreation of the 1976 Ibanez AD-200’s feedback network — including discrete 2N5457 JFETs in the regeneration path and capacitor-resistor ladder filtering calibrated to ±1.2% tolerance. This voicing system affects both dry signal coloration and repeat decay characteristics. In ‘Vintage’ mode, repeats exhibit pronounced low-mid bloom (peaking at 380 Hz) and accelerated high-end attenuation (−18 dB/octave above 5.1 kHz), closely matching oscilloscope traces captured from a serviced 1977 AD-200 unit.
